results.claim: 5-2-1 mutual authentication / 5-2-2 session-key confidentiality
results.procedure: honest handshake A<->B; compare Ksess, TH, both chains, KRA
results.expected: both accept with identical keys
results.observed: all identical = True

results.claim: 5-2-1 authentication of the initiator (MITM cannot substitute pkAe)
results.procedure: attacker with a valid key for ID C sends M1 structure under ID A
results.expected: Verify(IDA, M1, sigma) = 0
results.observed: aborted: Verify(params, IDA, M1, sigmaA) = 0 (eq 4-6)

results.claim: 5-2-5 impersonation using another node's identity key
results.procedure: corrupt an unrelated node C, run a full handshake with B as C
results.expected: C cannot make B believe it is talking to A
results.observed: B authenticated the peer as C, not A (no impersonation of A)
results.note: the authenticated id is carried in the transcript, so B's peer field is C

results.claim: 5-2-4 unknown key-share (UKS)
results.procedure: forward A's signed M1 to another node C
results.expected: M1 is bound to IDB inside sigma_A, so C must reject
results.observed: C aborted: Verify(params, IDA, M1, sigmaA) = 0 (eq 4-6)

results.claim: 5-2-3 replay resistance of the handshake
results.procedure: replay an already-consumed M1 to a fresh responder instance of B's identity, then hand the resulting M2 back to the original initiator
results.expected: responder rejects a replayed handshake; sessions must match
results.observed: fresh B accepted the stale M1 = False; None; B2 believes it shares a session with A (matching sessions = n/a, A's Ksess unchanged = n/a)
results.note: with the responder-side freshness rule of eq 4-6a in place - every NA it has answered is recorded for the node, and a repeated NA aborts before any key is derived - the stale M1 is refused by a fresh instance of the same identity, so no phantom session is attributed to the victim. This is the repair that closes F2; without the rule the same probe was accepted.

results.claim: 5-2-3 replay resistance of the ratchet layer
results.procedure: replay a consumed data message, replay it again after an asymmetric refresh, and deliver j=1 after j=2
results.expected: all three rejected
results.observed: same-epoch replay: replayed message (e=0, j=0) | cross-epoch replay: message from epoch 0 while in epoch 1 | counter going backwards: message counter went backwards (skipped key already erased)
results.note: skip-ahead is supported (keys for skipped indices are derived then erased), step-back is not - the price of eq 4-37 erasure

results.claim: 5-2-1 MITM: substituting handshake parameters
results.procedure: relay the handshake verbatim while holding a valid identity key of one's own, then try pkAe/NA/NB/ct0-derived keys against A's session key
results.expected: signature binding of pkAe makes substitution abort; wire data alone yields nothing
results.observed: handshake completed under relay=True; Ksess guessable from wire=False
results.note: pkAe is inside sigma_A (eq 4-4/4-5), so any substitution breaks verification

results.claim: 5-2-6 forward secrecy (PFS) across epochs
results.procedure: after 2 refreshes / 10 messages, leak B's {RK, CKs, CKr, epoch, TH} and try every recorded ciphertext, split by whether it predates the refresh the leaked state belongs to
results.expected: 0 of the 7 messages of earlier epochs openable
results.observed: 0/7 from earlier epochs open, 0/3 from the leaked epoch itself
results.note: cross-epoch PFS holds: rootKdf(RK_{e-1}, ss_e) (eq 4-31) is one-way and ss_e is a KEM secret the adversary cannot decapsulate. The messages of the leaked epoch are a separate claim - see b8

results.claim: 5-2-6 forward secrecy inside one epoch (epoch 0)
results.procedure: leak B's message_state at (e=0, next j=6) - both the chain-only attacker and the RK-aware attacker ProVerif derives; try the 5 past and 3 future ciphertexts
results.expected: past unreadable; future readable until the next asymmetric refresh
results.observed: chain-only: past 0/5, future 3/3  |  RK-aware: past 0/5, future 0/3
results.note: a symmetric chain still leaks forward from the exposure point until the KEM refresh repairs it, which is why the design is a dual ratchet; the RK side of the same scrape is closed for every epoch, including this one, because the chains are PRK leaves (eq 4-18/4-19 here, eq 4-32/4-33 after the amendment) rather than functions of the stored root key. Refreshed epochs behave the same way - see b8

results.claim: 5-2-6 forward secrecy inside the epoch that was scraped
results.procedure: run 5 messages in epoch 1, scrape B's message_state (which contains RK per eq 5-6), then re-derive the epoch's initial chain key per eq 4-32
results.expected: past messages of the epoch unreadable once their chain keys are erased (eq 4-37)
results.observed: chain-only attacker: past 0/5 | RK attacker: past 0/5, future 0/3, other epochs 0/3
results.note: eq 4-32/4-33 now seed the epoch's chains from PRK_e, the HKDF-Extract output of eq 4-31, while the stored RK is a sibling branch of the same extract; a scrape therefore cannot rebuild the epoch backwards, and the erasure of eq 4-37 is what bounds the damage. Residual, and stated as such: the same scrape still carries the live chain key, so messages after the exposure point of that epoch stay readable until the next asymmetric refresh repairs the root. This is the repair that closes F5.

results.claim: 5-2-6 post-compromise security (recovery)
results.procedure: leak state, let it go stale, run 3 asymmetric refreshes, then send traffic
results.expected: a stale snapshot must not open any post-refresh message
results.observed: 0/4 opened with stale state
results.note: conditional PCS: relies on a fresh sse the attacker cannot decapsulate

results.claim: 5-2-6 'exposure of the symmetric keys does not expose KRA'
results.procedure: leak {RK, CKs, CKr, epoch, TH}; try to recompute KRA from them
results.expected: KRA is derived from PRK0, not RK, so it is not reachable
results.observed: KRA recovered from leaked message state = False
results.note: this is the assumption the thesis rests on for refresh authenticity

results.claim: 5-2-6 / 5-3-2 PCS under the documented internal state StAL1
results.procedure: scrape node memory as specified in eq 5-5 (StAL1 = {skIBS, pkIBS_GW, RK0, KRA}), then forge a KEM refresh authenticated with the leaked KRA
results.expected: state exposure must not allow future compromise
results.observed: B accepted the forged refresh (e=1); attacker opened B's post-refresh plaintext = 1; A's next refresh aborted (epoch desynchronised)
results.note: the state model and the security claim contradict each other. Fix: keep KRA out of the scrapeable session state (secure element), or sign refreshes; see FINDINGS.md F3

results.claim: 5-2-2 session-key confidentiality under ephemeral reveal (eCK)
results.procedure: reveal only A's handshake KEM secret skAe, recompute ss0 -> PRK0 -> all epoch-0 keys; no long-term key is corrupted
results.expected: eCK requires the test session key to stay secret
results.observed: attacker recovered Ksess=True, RK=True, KRA=True from the session's own ephemeral alone
results.note: phase 1 binds ss0 to a single ephemeral contribution; NB is a plaintext salt. Fix: encapsulate to a responder KEM key as well and mix both secrets; see F4

results.claim: 5-2-6 repair after ephemeral compromise
results.procedure: same leak, then one asymmetric refresh; try to open post-refresh traffic with the stale PRK0 chain
results.expected: post-refresh traffic must be unreadable
results.observed: post-refresh opened with stale handshake state = False
results.note: the ratchet limits the damage window of an ephemeral reveal to one epoch

results.claim: recovery requires a *successful* refresh (stated assumption, ch.4-9)
results.procedure: jam every refresh message A->B, then let one data message through
results.expected: no security recovery while the control channel is jammed
results.observed: refresh jammed=True; traffic keeps flowing on the stale symmetric chain=True
results.note: the thesis explicitly disclaims PCS against a persistent active attacker

results.claim: 5-2-7 quantum resistance (no classical assumption on the wire)
results.procedure: enumerate the primitives actually used and their on-the-wire sizes
results.expected: only lattice + hash/symmetric primitives; no RSA/ECDH/ECDSA
results.observed: ML-KEM-512 pk=800 ct=768 ss=32 | ML-KEM-768 pk=1184 ct=1088 ss=32 | IBS: mpk=1568 usk=1536 sigma=1964 B | SHA3-256, HMAC-SHA3-256, HKDF-SHA3, AES-256-GCM
results.note: ch.5-2-7 names Kyber-768 for the ratchet layer; the harness measures both sizes. The signature is a rank-2 Module-LWE Fiat-Shamir-with-aborts prototype, not a NIST standard, so the claim inherits FIPS 203's assurance for the KEM only.

results.claim: 5-2-1 IBS unforgeability / PKG master-secret confidentiality
results.procedure: take one legitimately issued usk_id, divide it pointwise in the NTT domain by the public hash of that identity, then multiply the quotient by a different identity's hash and sign
results.expected: usk_id must reveal nothing about the master secret s1
results.observed: h invertible in 256/256 NTT slots; s1 recovered bit-exactly = True; forgery for an unissued identity verifies = True (honest signature still verifies = True)
results.note: the homomorphic (certificateless-style) key derivation usk_id = h*s1 is the leak: s1 is the PKG master secret and every node holds it. A GPV-style trapdoor derivation is required. See FINDINGS.md F1

results.claim: 5-2-8 key escrow is inherent to IBS (stated limitation)
results.procedure: the PKG, holding MSK, derives A's identity key and completes a handshake with B as A
results.expected: B accepts; escrow cannot be removed by this construction
results.observed: rogue-PKG session established = True
results.note: distinct from F1: escrow needs the MSK, F1 needs only one issued key

results.claim: 5-4-1 eq (11-5): the light tier's setup phase costs 5594 B, with |sigma| = 1964 B and a 1666 B non-signature term
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: rebuild eq (11-5) from the fields the reference code actually serialises (M1 + M2), separate the metadata term from the two signatures, and check the three numbers the amended section now prints
results.observed: metadata + KEM material = 1,666 B, |sigma| = 1,964 B, setup phase on the wire = 5,594 B
results.note: this row used to claim 2296 B at |sigma| = 300 B. Two corrections: the arithmetic constant is 1666 B, not the 1696 B the old substitution implied, and no 300 B signature comes out of ch.4-4 - the commitment (384 B at 6 bit/coeff) and the weight-39 challenge vector (44 B) already exceed 300 B before a response coefficient is sent, so the tier is priced with the signature the parameters actually produce. The equation itself is unchanged.

results.claim: 5-4-1: the proposed tier's setup phase costs 6506 B, i.e. 1666 B of material plus two 2420 B ML-DSA-44 signatures
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: the same reconstruction, substituting the standard signature the high tier names instead of an IBS of the same width
results.observed: with |sigma| = 2,420 B the layout gives 6,506 B; the identity-based signature of ch.4-4 would give 5,594 B
results.note: the old row said 6496 B at |sigma| = 2400 B. The thesis' arithmetic was 30 B off the metadata constant and the 2400 B signature is not a published size either; the tier now names ML-DSA-44 (2420 B) and the total follows.

results.claim: 5-4-1 eq (12-5) / table 5-3: a normal message costs 109 B of framing over its payload (epoch 4 + counter 8 + nonce 12 + bound context 69 + tag 16)
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: serialise one ratchet-layer data message exactly as the reference code does and split the transmitted framing from the payload
results.observed: 141 B on the wire for a 32 B payload = 109 B of framing: epoch 4 + counter 8 + nonce 12 + associated data 69 + ciphertext+tag 48
results.note: the row read 16 B, which is the AEAD tag on its own. Eq 4-34..4-36 also put the epoch and message counters (needed for key skipping), the AES-GCM nonce and the AD that binds the message to (IDA, IDB, e, j, TH) on the wire; the amended figure counts all of it. On 802.15.4 with a 127 B MAC payload the difference between 16 B and 109 B of framing is the difference between one frame and two, so the section states it as two.

results.claim: 5-4-1 eq (13-5) / tables 5-2 and 5-3: the asymmetric refresh costs 897 B + 865 B = 1762 B round trip
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: measure both refresh legs as the reference code emits them and account for the epoch number, the 61 B binding context and the lambda = 256 MAC that the KEM-only arithmetic leaves out
results.observed: A = 897 B (epoch 4 + AD 61 + pk 800 + MAC 32), B = 865 B (epoch 4 + AD 61 + ct 768 + MAC 32) = 1,762 B round trip
results.note: the old figure was 816 + 784 = 1600 B: the KEM material plus a 16 B MAC. Eq 4-25/4-26 add a 61 B epoch-binding context and a 4 B epoch number to each leg, and lambda = 256 makes the MAC 32 B rather than 16 B - 81 B per leg, 162 B over the round trip.

results.claim: 5-7 / table 5-3: the light tier's setup phase (5594 B) is above PiLike [8] (3860 B) and AKAME [4] (4160 B), and the design's advantage is the cumulative one of e6
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: put the measured handshake of this design on the same footing as the competitor figures quoted in table 5-3 and check the ordering the amended row states
results.expected: heavier at setup, lighter per message
results.observed: measured 5,594 B = +45% against PiLike [8] (3,860 B) and +34% against AKAME [4] (4,160 B)
results.note: the row used to claim the opposite ordering, at 2296 B. The single-phase comparison genuinely goes against this design once the signature it actually produces is priced; what it wins is every later leg, which neither competitor has (the same table says they 'require re-running the key agreement'), so the comparison is stated per phase and summed in e6 rather than claimed in one snapshot.

results.claim: 5-7 / table 5-3, read cumulatively: this design beats schemes that must re-run the key agreement for every message
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: price one session of k messages twice - this design (setup + k data messages + a refresh every 100 messages) against the competitor figures of table 5-3 multiplied by k, since those designs have no ratchet layer
results.expected: lower total bytes over a session
results.observed: k=10: ours 7,004 B, PiLike 38,600 B, AKAME 41,600 B | k=100: ours 21,456 B, PiLike 386,000 B, AKAME 416,000 B | k=1000: ours 164,214 B, PiLike 3,860,000 B, AKAME 4,160,000 B
results.note: the ratchet is real and it is the claim worth keeping: setup is already 1,734 B heavier than PiLike's single handshake, and the crossover is at k = 2 messages, after which every additional message costs 141 B here against 3,860 B there. Table 5-3 as printed compares only the setup snapshot and therefore understates its own case. One honest caveat on the modelling: the competitor column prices 're-runs the key agreement' (the thesis' own words in that row) as a full setup handshake per message; a design that re-authenticates with a signature only would cost 2,420 B per message instead and would push the crossover to k = 3.

results.claim: 5-5: long-term key memory is 2368 B (usk_id 1536 B + KEM public key 800 B + KRA 32 B) and 3936 B once the group public key a verifier must hold is counted
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: measure the identity key and the group public key ch.4-4's parameters actually produce, then add the 800 B KEM public key and the 32 B KRA the thesis lists
results.observed: usk = 1,536 B (L=2 vectors of n=256 coefficients at 3 B = 2*256*3), own key + KEM pk + KRA = 2,368 B, plus mpk = 1,568 B gives 3,936 B
results.note: the section said 1856 B, built on a 1024 B identity key. Ch.4-4's expansion is L vectors of n coefficients, 3 B per coefficient, so 1536 B; and the group public key was not counted at all although every Verify needs it. The 800 B KEM term was right.

results.claim: 5-5: the double ratchet needs 180 B of live session state, 212 B if KRA is kept in RAM alongside it
results.model: byte accounting of the reference implementation
results.procedure: count everything a running session must keep in order to send, receive, skip ahead and authenticate a refresh, per eq 4-11..4-36
results.observed: 180 B as implemented, 212 B with KRA in RAM. The state is RK, CK^send, CK^recv, TH, the epoch number, both message counters and the received-index set
results.note: 104 B is reachable only by dropping the transcript binding, and that binding is what makes eq 4-26's refresh authentication and the UKS resistance of 5-2-4 work. The amended figure also states the KRA rule of 5-2-6: KRA belongs to the long-term key store, and the 212 B figure is what a node pays if it keeps it in the session state instead - which is exactly the exposure eq 5-5 documents.

results.claim: 5-6 / table 5-2: phase-1 operation sets - initiator = TKeyGen+TDecaps+TSign+TVerify+TKDF, responder = TEncaps+TSign+TVerify+TKDF
results.model: operation counting in the reference implementation, priced with native cycles
results.procedure: instrument KEM.KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps, IBS.sign/verify, HKDF, HMAC, Hash and AEAD and drive the three handshake legs separately, attributing every call to the role that made it; then price each role's set with c/ibs.c and the ML-KEM-512 measurements
results.expected: A: 1 keygen, 1 decaps, 1 sign, 1 verify; B: 1 encaps, 1 sign, 1 verify, no keygen
results.observed: A = IBS.sign=1, IBS.verify=1, KEM.Decaps=1, KEM.KeyGen=1 ; B = IBS.sign=1, IBS.verify=1, KEM.Encaps=1 ; priced: A 2,262,803 cycles, B 2,152,528 cycles (A/B = 1.05)
results.note: the sets are exactly as table 5-2 says, and the asymmetry it implies is real but small: signing is 77% of A's priced phase-1 cost and 81% of B's, so the extra keygen that makes A 'heavier' moves the total by 5.1%. The only lever this table leaves is A's ephemeral keygen (245,137 cycles), which an idle initiator could generate in advance; the responder already does no keygen.

results.claim: 5-4-2 eq (16-5) / table 5-4: a normal message performs no asymmetric operation, reducing the cost from matrix multiplication to a constant KDF cost
results.model: operation counting in the reference implementation
results.procedure: count every primitive invoked while 20 messages are sent and received inside one epoch
results.expected: 0 asymmetric operations per message
results.observed: 0 asymmetric calls in 20 message pairs; per message pair: AEAD=2, HKDF-Expand=4, HMAC=4, Hash=1
results.note: the design's strongest measured property, and it holds exactly: a message pair is 4 HKDF-Expand + 1 hash + 2 AEAD contexts and nothing else (the HMAC column counts the PRF calls the KDF makes internally, one per expansion, so it is not additional work). Two caveats worth stating in the thesis: the 'constant' KDF cost is per message and per direction - 4 expansions, not the 2 that eq 4-34/4-35 suggest read one-way - and AES-256-GCM is not the lightweight choice the framing implies, since a hardware-less M0 has to run it in software.

results.claim: 5-4-2 eq (17-5) / table 5-2: the asymmetric refresh removes Sign/Verify and costs one KEM triple plus HMACs
results.model: operation counting in the reference implementation, priced with native cycles
results.procedure: run one full epoch refresh - MsgA, MsgB and the return leg - with the primitive counters installed
results.expected: no IBS.sign / IBS.verify anywhere in the refresh
results.observed: HKDF-Expand=6, HKDF-Extract=2, HMAC=12, Hash=2, KEM.Decaps=1, KEM.Encaps=1, KEM.KeyGen=1 -> sign+verify calls = 0
results.note: confirmed, and it is why the amortisation of section 5-4-2 works: a refresh is 638,719 cycles of KEM where a re-handshake would be 4,415,331 cycles. Of the 12 HMAC calls, 6 are the PRF inside the 6 HKDF-Expand invocations and 6 are the explicit eq 4-26/4-29 refresh tags - the MACs that replace the signatures. F3 (RESULTS.md, claim 17) shows what that trade costs if KRA is left in the state an attacker can scrape.

results.claim: 5-7 / table 5-4: the rank-2 identity-based signature costs 72% of ML-DSA-44 for key generation and 69% for verification, but 148% for signing - the handshake is cheaper with a standard signature
results.model: native cycles (c/ibs.c on the Dilithium ring vs the Dilithium-2 reference)
results.procedure: compare measured mean cycles of one accepted signature, of one verification and of one key pair, on the same ring (n=256, q=8380417), same machine, with message-varying rejection loops in both
results.observed: keygen 265,095 cycles = 72% of Dilithium-2's; verify 153,768 = 69%; sign 1,734,538 = 148% of a Dilithium-2 signature (1,168,306)
results.note: table 5-4 formerly argued that K = L = 2 makes the identity-based signature cheap enough to place in phase 1. The dimensional argument holds for keygen and verification and fails for signing: beta = (tau-1)*W_H*eta+1 = 609 against Dilithium's 78 puts the per-attempt acceptance at 0.037 instead of 0.432, i.e. 26.7 rejection attempts per signature against 2.3. The cost sits in the homomorphic key derivation, not in the ring, so any construction that keeps usk_id = h*s1 inherits it.

results.claim: 5-5: the persistent footprint is 2548 B (4116 B with the group public key), which the section places on a Cortex-M4-class node with 48 kB of SRAM - not on a class-1 part
results.model: capacity arithmetic from the reference implementation + pqm4's published M4 figures
results.procedure: add up what a node must hold in RAM (identity key, KEM public key, KRA, session state, group public key) against the budget the amended section names, and read the handshake cost from pqm4
results.expected: 4116 B against a 48 kB budget
results.observed: 2,368 B of key material, 2,548 B with the session state, 4,116 B once the group public key the verifier must hold is counted - 8.4% of a 48 kB budget, before code, stack, the NTT working buffers or the AES-GCM context
results.note: the section's conclusion used to read 'less than 2.0 kB, therefore runnable on class-1 Cortex-M0/M3 parts'. Its own byte counts refuse that: the persistent state alone is 1.25x a 2 kB budget before a single byte of working memory, and pqm4 prices a full ML-KEM-512 + ML-DSA-44 handshake at about 498 ms on a Cortex-M4 with a refresh at 50.5 ms, so the amended text names the M4 class and states that the two phase-one signatures dominate; class-1 nodes stay on the ch.4-6 layer-1 profile, which stops after the KEM.
